claim: It has been assumed that parkin-dependent mitophagy follows a similar mechanism to yeast steady-state mitophagy.
source: As steady-state mitophagy in yeast requires mitochondria-ER contacts (Böckler and Westermann, 2014), it has been assumed that parkin-dependent mitophagy follows a similar mechanism (Yoshii and Mizushima, 2015).

claim: PINK1 and parkin may regulate contact between mitochondria and the ER during mitophagy.

claim: Studies demonstrate high levels of parkin ubiquitination activity on Mfn2 in both cells and in organello ubiquitination assays.

evidence: Supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2017

claim: Parkin decreases the total length of ER-OMM contact in CCCP-treated U2OS:GFP-parkin cells.
source: We quantified ER tubules within 100 nm of the OMM, as this distance is enough to capture tubules closely associated with the OMM (Figure 1A, left panel and inset). To induce PINK1-/parkin-mediated mitophagy, we treated U2OS cells stably-expressing GFP-parkin (U2OS:GFP-parkin) and control U2OS:GFP cells with CCCP for four hours, and observed by EM a decrease the total length of ER-OMM contact in both cell lines, although this decrease was greater in magnitude in cells expressing GFP-parkin (Figure 1A, quantified in 1B).
evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B

claim: Parkin has a specific effect on reducing the percentage of the OMM that remains in contact with the ER in depolarized cells.
source: However, when CCCP-induced, parkin-independent mitochondrial fragmentation was taken into account (Figure 1C), parkin had a specific effect on reducing the percentage of the OMM that remained in contact with the ER in depolarized cells (Figure 1D), as well as the percentage of total mitochondria that were still connected to the ER (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and 1E

claim: Parkin reduces the percentage of total mitochondria that are connected to the ER in depolarized cells.
source: However, when CCCP-induced, parkin-independent mitochondrial fragmentation was taken into account (Figure 1C), parkin had a specific effect on reducing the percentage of the OMM that remained in contact with the ER in depolarized cells (Figure 1D), as well as the percentage of total mitochondria that were still connected to the ER (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and 1E

claim: Parkin disrupts mitochondria-ER contact upon activation of mitophagy.
source: This effect was robust, as repeating our quantification using a variety of interorganellar tethering lengths – ER-OMM distances of 100, 50 and 25 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) – pointed us to the same conclusion; parkin disrupts mitochondria-ER contact upon activation of mitophagy.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: The subsets of remaining contacts after parkin-mediated reduction are biased towards longer interorganellar distances.
source: Moreover, the subsets of remaining contacts observed after the ~75% reduction in CCCP-treated, GFP-parkin-expressing cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) were biased towards longer interorganellar distances (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), consistent with parkin driving the OMM and ER apart.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Parkin ablates contact between mitochondria and the ER as an early step during depolarization-induced mitophagy in cells.
source: Given that the mitochondria observed in our EM analyses were still intact organelles and not yet engulfed by the isolation membrane (IM) of the autophagosome (Figure 1A, right panel), we concluded that parkin ablates contact between mitochondria and the ER as an early step during depolarization-induced mitophagy in cells.
evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 1A

claim: MG132 co-incubation rescued ER-OMM contact in U2OS:GFP-parkin cells treated with CCCP.
source: MG132 co-incubation rescued ER-OMM contact in U2OS:GFP-parkin cells treated with CCCP (Figure 1H,I and J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H, I, and J

claim: PINK1 depletion prevents OMM-ER disruption in CCCP-treated cells.
source: As expected, we also prevented OMM-ER disruption in cells depleted of PINK1 (Figure 1H,I and J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H, I, and J

claim: CCCP induces Mfn2 ubiquitination in control iDA neurons but not in parkin deletion neurons.
source: Upon treatment of these neurons with CCCP for only one hour, we observed Mfn2 ubiquitination in both control lines but not in the parkin deletion line (Figure 1M).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1M

claim: CCCP induces a decrease in <100 nm ER-OMM appositions in control iDA neurons but not in parkin deletion neurons.
source: When we analyzed mitochondria-ER appositions in these cells, we again observed a CCCP-dependent decrease in the amount of <100 nm ER-OMM appositions in both control lines (Figure 1N and O). However, this decrease was absent in the parkin deletion line (Figure 1N and O), supporting our previous overexpression data in U2OS cells (Figure 1A to E ).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1N and O

claim: PINK1 and parkin function to destroy contacts between the ER and mitochondria during mitophagy.
source: Thus, PINK1 and parkin function to destroy contacts between the ER and mitochondria during mitophagy, likely through parkin-mediated OMM protein ubiquitination and turnover, as this process can be prevented by inhibiting proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Supported by data from multiple experiments showing PINK1/parkin-dependent ER-OMM contact disruption that is blocked by proteasome inhibition

claim: ER-mitochondria uncoupling occurs as an early step in the mitophagy pathway, prior to autophagosomal engulfment of the organelle.
source: Our EM data demonstrated that ER-mitochondria uncoupling occurs as an early step in the mitophagy pathway, prior to autophagosomal engulfment of the organelle (Figure 1F), and we sought to understand the underlying mechanism of this phenomenon.
evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Turnover of both Mfn1 and Mfn2 occurred early (almost complete disappearance by two hours) compared to other OMM proteins during CCCP treatment.
source: Turnover of both Mfn1 and Mfn2 occurred early (almost complete disappearance by two hours) compared to other OMM proteins (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: A rapid 'burst' of Mfn2 ubiquitination occurs between 30 and 60 min CCCP treatment.
source: Upon higher exposure (Figure 2B) of these immunoblots (from Figure 2A), we observed a rapid 'burst' of Mfn2 ubiquitination that occurred between 30 and 60 min CCCP.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2B

claim: TOM20 ubiquitination occurs gradually over a period of hours, rather than rapidly over a period of minutes.
source: When compared to TOM20, a protein that is not promptly ubiquitinated by parkin (Sarraf et al., 2013), the rapidity of this Ub burst on Mfn2 was emphasized as TOM20 ubiquitination occurs gradually over a period of hours, rather than rapidly over a period of minutes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Sarraf et al., 2013

claim: Ubiquitination of the mitofusins is one of the very first steps after the induction of mitophagy.
source: Thus, ubiquitination of the mitofusins is one of the very first steps after the induction of mitophagy.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid ubiquitination kinetics of Mfn1 and Mfn2 compared to other OMM proteins

claim: Robust coimmunoprecipitation of ubiquitinated Mfn1 and Mfn2 with GFP-parkinWT occurs at one hour CCCP.
source: We observed robust coimmunoprecipitation of ubiquitinated Mfn1 and Mfn2 with GFP-parkinWT at one hour CCCP (corresponding to the Ub burst observed in Figure 2B), with no apparent binding at four hours (Figure 2C), likely due to turnover of the Mfns by the proteasome at this time (Figures 1G and 2B and [Tanaka et al., 2010]).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Ubiquitinated Miro1 binds to WT parkin only at four hours of CCCP treatment.
source: When we analyzed other parkin substrates that are ubiquitinated less rapidly than the Mfns (Figure 2A), we observed binding to WT parkin only at four hours of CCCP treatment in the case of ubiquitinated Miro1, and binding of mono-ubiquitinated HK1 at one hour CCCP, which was further shifted at four hours, indicative of processivity of HK1 ubiquitination (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Mono-ubiquitinated HK1 binds to WT parkin at one hour CCCP, which is further shifted at four hours, indicative of processivity of HK1 ubiquitination.
source: When we analyzed other parkin substrates that are ubiquitinated less rapidly than the Mfns (Figure 2A), we observed binding to WT parkin only at four hours of CCCP treatment in the case of ubiquitinated Miro1, and binding of mono-ubiquitinated HK1 at one hour CCCP, which was further shifted at four hours, indicative of processivity of HK1 ubiquitination (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claim: None of the ubiquitinated species coimmunoprecipitated with GFP-parkinA320R.
source: None of these ubiquitinated species coimmunoprecipitated with GFP-parkinA320R (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C

claim: GFP-parkin binds ubiquitinated Mfn2.
source: To confirm that GFP-parkin was indeed binding ubiquitinated Mfn2, we treated GFP-parkin immunoprecipitates from CCCP-treated cells with Usp2 deubiquitinase (see schematic in Figure 2D), which is active on both phosphorylated and unphosphorylated Ub chains (Wauer et al., 2015b), and observed the release of Mfn2 from the parkin-bound bead fraction into the supernatant after separation by centrifugation (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by on-bead deubiquitination data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Early on in the mitophagy pathway, parkin binds ubiquitinated Mfn2, likely through interactions with pUb moieties.
source: These results strongly suggested that, early on in the mitophagy pathway, parkin was binding ubiquitinated Mfn2, likely through interactions with pUb moieties.
evidence: Inferred from coimmunoprecipitation and deubiquitination experiments

claim: Mfn2 immunoprecipitation from CCCP-treated U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells contains Ub-modified species.
source: When we immunoprecipitated Mfn2 from U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells that were treated with CCCP for one hour, we detected Ub-modified species by immunoblot (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2F

claim: LC/MS confirmed that the Mfn2 immunoprecipitation contained pS65 Ub selectively in the CCCP-treated condition.
source: Liquid-chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (LC/MS) confirmed that the Mfn2 immunoprecipitation contained pS65 Ub selectively in the CCCP-treated condition (Figure 2G), despite lower Mfn2 levels (Figure 2A and F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Both pS65 and unphosphorylated Ub are covalently attached to Mfn2.
source: We then confirmed that both pS65 and unphosphorylated Ub were covalently attached to Mfn2 by its precipitation under denaturing conditions and detecting pS65 Ub and total Ub by immunoblot (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by denaturing immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2H

claim: pS65 Ub, Ub and (shifted) Mfn2 can be detected in GST-R0RBRWT pulldowns in a CCCP-dependent manner.
source: In a CCCP-dependent manner, pS65 Ub, Ub and (shifted) Mfn2 could be detected in GST-R0RBRWT pulldowns (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2J

claim: pS65 Ub, Ub and Mfn2 are not observed in pulldowns using GST-R0RBRA320R.
source: Strikingly, we did not observe any of these factors in pulldowns using GST-R0RBRA320R (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2J

claim: Mfn2 is phosphoubiquitinated during mitochondrial depolarization.
source: Mfn2 is therefore phosphoubiquitinated and, taken together with our previous data, a burst of phosphoubiquitination – parkin-mediated ubiquitination coupled to PINK1-catalyzed phosphorylation – occurs on Mfn2 at an early time point in the mitophagy pathway.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments including LC/MS, denaturing IP, and GST pulldowns

claim: A burst of phosphoubiquitination occurs on Mfn2 at an early time point in the mitophagy pathway.
source: Mfn2 is therefore phosphoubiquitinated and, taken together with our previous data, a burst of phosphoubiquitination – parkin-mediated ubiquitination coupled to PINK1-catalyzed phosphorylation – occurs on Mfn2 at an early time point in the mitophagy pathway.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing rapid Mfn2 ubiquitination and phosphoubiquitination

claim: Mfn2 silencing increases mitochondrial fragmentation in U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells.
source: We confirmed Mfn1 and Mfn2 depletion by immunoblot (Figure 3A), and observed mitochondrial fragmentation in both siMfn1 and siMfn2 cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) with an ER-OMM apposition defect unique to the siMfn2 condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C and D), as expected.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Mfn2 silencing causes an ER-OMM apposition defect.
source: We confirmed Mfn1 and Mfn2 depletion by immunoblot (Figure 3A), and observed mitochondrial fragmentation in both siMfn1 and siMfn2 cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) with an ER-OMM apposition defect unique to the siMfn2 condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C and D), as expected.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C and D

claim: Mfn2 silencing increases the kinetics of parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria.
source: Remarkably, we observed faster mitochondrial recruitment in siMfn2 (but not siMfn1) cells, under both bioenergetic conditions (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by parkin recruitment data shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: Mfn2 silencing increases parkin recruitment in galactose-grown cells to levels seen in glucose-maintained cells transfected with control siRNA.
source: Strikingly, Mfn2 silencing increased recruitment in galactose-grown cells to levels seen in glucose-maintained cells transfected with control siRNA (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by parkin recruitment data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Silencing Mfn1 and Mfn2 simultaneously does not further enhance the kinetics of parkin recruitment beyond single, Mfn2-depleted cells.
source: Silencing Mfn1 and Mfn2 simultaneously (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) did not further enhance the kinetics of parkin recruitment beyond single, Mfn2-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D), implying that this phenotype was Mfn2-specific and unrelated to a loss of mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D

claim: The increased parkin recruitment phenotype in Mfn2-depleted cells is Mfn2-specific and unrelated to a loss of mitochondrial fusion.
source: Silencing Mfn1 and Mfn2 simultaneously (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) did not further enhance the kinetics of parkin recruitment beyond single, Mfn2-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D), implying that this phenotype was Mfn2-specific and unrelated to a loss of mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that double knockdown does not enhance the phenotype beyond Mfn2 single knockdown

claim: Silencing of PACS2 or Stx17 increases the translocation of parkin to mitochondria.
source: When we tested parkin recruitment in these cells, we saw that, similarly to Mfn2 knockdown, silencing of either PACS2 (siPACS2) or Stx17 (siStx17) increased the translocation of parkin to mitochondria (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and H

claim: Disruption of mitochondrion-ER tethering increases the kinetics of parkin translocation to depolarized mitochondria.
source: Thus, disruption of mitochondrion-ER tethering increases the kinetics of parkin translocation to depolarized mitochondria.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing increased parkin recruitment upon silencing of Mfn2, PACS2, and Stx17

claim: In Mfn2-depleted cells, depolarization-induced mitophagy is enhanced.
source: These data demonstrate that, in Mfn2-depleted cells, depolarization-induced mitophagy is enhanced, in line with our parkin recruitment experiments (Figure 3A to E), and demonstrate that Mfn2 represses mitophagy at the level of pathway initiation.
evidence: Supported by mtKeima data shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: Mfn2 represses mitophagy at the level of pathway initiation.
source: These data demonstrate that, in Mfn2-depleted cells, depolarization-induced mitophagy is enhanced, in line with our parkin recruitment experiments (Figure 3A to E), and demonstrate that Mfn2 represses mitophagy at the level of pathway initiation.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced mitophagy and faster parkin recruitment in Mfn2-depleted cells

claim: Mfn2 KO cells display increased recruitment kinetics of GFP-parkin.
source: Corroborating our earlier data in siMfn2 cells, Mfn2 KO cells (grown on glucose) transiently transfected with GFP-parkin displayed increased recruitment kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F) and increased mitophagy (Figure 3—figure supplement 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F

claim: Mfn2 KO cells display increased mitophagy.
source: Corroborating our earlier data in siMfn2 cells, Mfn2 KO cells (grown on glucose) transiently transfected with GFP-parkin displayed increased recruitment kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F) and increased mitophagy (Figure 3—figure supplement 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4G and H

claim: Parkin translocation in Mfn2 KO cells remains PINK1-dependent.

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A-D

claim: Cells expressing GFP-parkinA320R fail to translocate under conditions of Mfn2-depletion.
source: Moreover, cells expressing GFP-parkinA320R (Figure 3—figure supplement 5E) failed to translocate under conditions of Mfn2-depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5F and G

claim: Mfn2 reduction increases on-pathway mitophagy kinetics.
source: This indicates a clear requirement for PINK1 and Ub phosphorylation for parkin translocation in Mfn2-depleted cells, demonstrating that Mfn2 reduction increases on-pathway mitophagy kinetics.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for PINK1 and pUb-binding for parkin translocation in Mfn2-depleted cells

claim: Mitochondria-ER contact is dispensable for mitophagy.
source: Taken together, our data not only show that mitochondria-ER contact is dispensable for mitophagy, but that this type of organellar coupling in fact antagonizes the pathway.
evidence: Inferred from data showing enhanced mitophagy upon disruption of mitochondria-ER contacts

claim: Mitochondria-ER tethering antagonizes mitophagy.
source: Taken together, our data not only show that mitochondria-ER contact is dispensable for mitophagy, but that this type of organellar coupling in fact antagonizes the pathway.
evidence: Inferred from data showing enhanced mitophagy upon disruption of mitochondria-ER contacts

claim: Ectopic expression of Mfn2, but not Mfn1, suppresses the recruitment of YFP-parkin to depolarized mitochondria in Mfn2 KO cells.
source: Turning to recruitment assays – in which we observed faster GFP-parkin recruitment in Mfn2 KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F) – we observed that ectopic expression of Mfn2, but not Mfn1, was able to suppress the recruitment of YFP-parkin to depolarized mitochondria (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: The antagonistic effect of Mfn2 on mitophagy occurs through its ability to tether mitochondria to the ER and not its effect on mitochondrial fusion.
source: This is in line with our previous data showing that the antagonistic effect of Mfn2 on mitophagy occurs through its ability to tether mitochondria to the ER (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H–J) and not its effect on mitochondrial fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D and 3H-J

claim: Mutation of K406, K416 and K420 in the HR1 domain (Mfn2HR1) reduces CCCP-induced ubiquitination of Mfn2 by ~75%.
source: We thus posited that mutation of several lysine residues would likely be required to reduce Mfn2 ubiquitination. While mutation of all major sites of Mfn2 ubiquitination almost completely abolishes its modification by parkin (Heo et al., 2015), we found that mutation of K406, K416 and K420 in the HR1 domain (Mfn2HR1) reduced its CCCP-induced ubiquitination by ~75%, as measured by the disappearance of the unmodified band by immunoblot (Figure 4E and F; here Mfn2 levels are normalized to the untreated condition for each construct).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: Mutation of all four sites in HR2 (Mfn2HR2) fails to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification.
source: This effect was greater than what we observed with the single mutant, Mfn2K406R (K416 and K420 appear dispensable in this assay), and mutation of all four sites in HR2 (Mfn2HR2) or the double T111A/S442A phosphomutant (Mfn2TS/AA) failed to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: The double T111A/S442A phosphomutant (Mfn2TS/AA) fails to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification.
source: This effect was greater than what we observed with the single mutant, Mfn2K406R (K416 and K420 appear dispensable in this assay), and mutation of all four sites in HR2 (Mfn2HR2) or the double T111A/S442A phosphomutant (Mfn2TS/AA) failed to significantly reduce Mfn2 modification (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: Mfn2HR1, Mfn2HR2 and Mfn2T111A/S442A rescue mitochondrial morphology in a similar manner to WT Mfn2.
source: Introduction of either Mfn2HR1, Mfn2HR2 or Mfn2T111A/S442A into Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkin cells rescued morphology in a similar manner to WT Mfn2 (Figure 4H), demonstrating these mutations did not disrupt mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4H

claim: All three Mfn2 mutants (HR1, HR2 and T111A/S442A) form HMW complexes similar to WT.
source: By blue native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (BN-PAGE), we observed that all three mutants (HR1, HR2 and T111A/S442A) formed HMW complexes similar to WT in solubilized mitochondria (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 4I

claim: Only rescue of Mfn2 with Mfn2HR1 blocks the turnover of mitochondria in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells.
source: When we assayed mitophagy in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells, we found that only rescue of Mfn2 with Mfn2HR1 – the ubiquitination of which is compromised (Figure 4E and F) – blocked the turnover of mitochondria (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4J and K

claim: Ubiquitination of the Mfn2 HR1 domain by parkin is required for efficient mitophagy.
source: Thus, ubiquitination of the Mfn2 HR1 domain by parkin is required for efficient mitophagy and, taken together with our previous mitophagic data in Mfn2-depleted cells, demonstrates that parkin and PINK1 directly counter Mfn2-mediated mitochondria-ER tethering through Mfn2 turnover to promote mitophagy.
evidence: Inferred from data showing that Mfn2HR1 blocks mitophagy

claim: Parkin and PINK1 directly counter Mfn2-mediated mitochondria-ER tethering through Mfn2 turnover to promote mitophagy.
source: Thus, ubiquitination of the Mfn2 HR1 domain by parkin is required for efficient mitophagy and, taken together with our previous mitophagic data in Mfn2-depleted cells, demonstrates that parkin and PINK1 directly counter Mfn2-mediated mitochondria-ER tethering through Mfn2 turnover to promote mitophagy.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing Mfn2 ubiquitination, turnover, and effects on mitophagy

claim: Mfn2 exists in a bimodal distribution into two complexes, weighing approximately ~250 kDa and ~500 kDa.
source: Examining HMW complexes by BN-PAGE in untreated U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells (expressing endogenous Mfn2), we observed a bimodal distribution of Mfn2 into two complexes, weighing approximately ~250 kDa and ~500 kDa (Figure 5A, leftmost lane, similar to what was seen in Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Mfn1 only forms a ~ 250 kDa HMW complex.
source: By contrast, Mfn1 – which, in our assays, appears dispensable for mitochondria-ER tethering as assayed by EM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and its effect on parkin recruitment (Figure 3C–E) – only formed a ~ 250 kDa HMW complex (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The ~500 kDa complex containing solely Mfn2 is a dimer of the ~250 kDa Mfn2-containing subcomplex that potentially bridges the ER and OMM.
source: We thus considered the ~500 kDa complex containing solely Mfn2 as a dimer of the ~250 kDa Mfn2-containing subcomplex that potentially bridges the ER and OMM.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Mfn2 uniquely forms a ~500 kDa complex and its known role in ER-OMM tethering

claim: CCCP treatment causes a rapid loss of Mfn2- (and Mfn1-) containing HMW complexes.
source: Upon CCCP treatment, we observed a rapid loss Mfn2- (and Mfn1-) containing complexes (Figure 5A), concomitant with its phosphoubiquitination (Figure 2) and dependent upon parkin ligase activity (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C

claim: The disappearance of HMW Mfn complexes is predominantly due to their extraction from the OMM.
source: While treatment of mitochondrial lysates with Usp2 deubiquitinase slightly increased levels of the unmodified Mfn1 or Mfn2 band in mitochondria isolated from CCCP-treated cells (Figure 5D; the densitometry measurements correspond to the shorter exposures of Mfn1 and Mfn2), this was not to levels seen in mitochondria from untreated cells. This result indicated that the disappearance of HMW Mfn complexes are predominantly due to their extraction from the OMM (and not a high level of modification by Ub).
evidence: Supported by Usp2 treatment data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Extraction of HMW Mfn complexes is mediated by the AAA-ATPase p97/VCP.
source: This process is thought to be mediated by the AAA-ATPase p97/VCP (Tanaka et al., 2010) and, accordingly, when we treated U2OS:GFP-parkinWT cells with CCCP in the presence of the non-competitive p97 inhibitor NMS-873 (Magnaghi et al., 2013), extraction of HMW complexes containing either Mfn1 or Mfn2 was accordingly repressed (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2010 and data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Both ~250 kDa (containing Mfn1 and/or Mfn2) and ~500 kDa (Mfn2 only) complexes are stabilized in the presence of NMS-873.
source: Indeed, both ~250 kDa (containing Mfn1 and/or Mfn2) and ~500 kDa (Mfn2 only) complexes were stabilized in the presence of NMS-873 (Figure 5E), with smearing occurring due to Mfn ubiquitination (see Figure 2), indicating that parkin-mediated ubiquitination itself was not sufficient to drive apart the ~500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge.
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Parkin-mediated ubiquitination itself is not sufficient to drive apart the ~500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge.
source: Indeed, both ~250 kDa (containing Mfn1 and/or Mfn2) and ~500 kDa (Mfn2 only) complexes were stabilized in the presence of NMS-873 (Figure 5E), with smearing occurring due to Mfn ubiquitination (see Figure 2), indicating that parkin-mediated ubiquitination itself was not sufficient to drive apart the ~500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ubiquitinated Mfn2 complexes remain intact when p97 is inhibited

claim: p97 inhibition prevents the dissociation of mitochondria from the ER during mitophagy.
source: Analysis of OMM-ER appositions in these cells revealed that p97 inhibition prevented the dissociation of mitochondria from the ER (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 5F-H

claim: p97-dependent extraction of Mfn2 HMW complexes from the OMM separates mitochondria from the ER during mitophagy.
source: Thus, p97-dependent extraction of Mfn2 HMW complexes from the OMM separates mitochondria from the ER during mitophagy.
evidence: Inferred from data showing that p97 inhibition prevents both Mfn2 complex extraction and ER-OMM dissociation

claim: NMS-873 co-incubation completely blocks the mitochondrial translocation of p97 in CCCP-treated cells.
source: Consistent with our HMW complex extraction data (Figure 5E), co-incubation of cells with CCCP and NMS-873 completely blocked the mitochondrial translocation of p97 (Figure 6A and B) which occurs during mitophagy (Kimura et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B and citations to Kimura et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2010

claim: p97 depletion increases ubiquitinated Mfn2 upon depolarization.
source: We observed a similar effect when we silenced p97 with siRNA (sip97); in p97-depleted cells treated with CCCP, we saw an increase in ubiquitinated Mfn2 upon depolarization (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Basal levels of Mfn2 increase upon prolonged p97 depletion.
source: Additionally, basal levels of Mfn2 increased upon prolonged p97 depletion (Figure 6E), consistent with the possible involvement of p97 in steady-state Mfn2 turnover (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6E and citation to Zhang et al., 2017

claim: NMS-873 stabilizes ubiquitinated Mfn2 in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells rescued with WT Mfn2.
source: In Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells rescued with WT Mfn2, CCCP induced Mfn2 turnover and, when cells were co-incubated with NMS-873, we observed a stabilization of ubiquitinated Mfn2 (Figure 6F) similar to WT U2OS cells expressing GFP-parkin (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Mfn2HR1 shows a severe reduction in NMS-873-dependent stabilization of CCCP-induced Mfn2-Ub conjugates.
source: When we expressed Mfn2HR1 in Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells, we observed a severe reduction in NMS-873-dependent stabilization of CCCP-induced Mfn2-Ub conjugates (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Ubiquitination of lysines in the Mfn2 HR1 domain is recognized by p97 and signals for extraction of the protein.
source: We confirmed this reduction in ubiquitination by immunoprecipiting Mfn2 from reconstituted cells treated with CCCP and NMS-873 under denaturing conditions and immunoblotting for Ub (Figure 6G). This supports our mutagenesis data showing a reduction of Mfn2HR1 turnover (Figure 4E and F) and is mechanistically consistent with ubiquitination of lysines in the Mfn2 HR1 domain being recognized by p97 and signaling for extraction of the protein.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6G and inferred from mutagenesis data

claim: Ubiquitinated Mfn2 is not the sole p97-binding protein on the OMM.
source: While we posited that Mfn2 may be acting as a p97 receptor during mitophagy, we observed robust p97 recruitment in depolarized Mfn2 KO:YFP-parkinWT cells (Figure 6H and I). Moreover, p97 recruitment was similar in cells expressing either Mfn2WT or Mfn2HR1 (Figure 6H and I). p97 recruitment levels in both Mfn2 rescue conditions were lower than in cells transfected with empty vector (Figure 6H and I) likely owing to the delayed parkin recruitment kinetics in Mfn2-expressing cells (Figure 4B and C). Thus, ubiquitinated Mfn2 is not the sole p97-binding protein on the OMM.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6H and I

claim: The interaction between parkin and ubiquitinated Mfn2 is stabilized when cells are co-treated with CCCP and NMS-873.
source: As we detected pUb conjugated to immunoprecipitated Mfn2 from cells treated with CCCP (Figure 2G and H), we co-treated cells with CCCP and NMS-873 and observed that the interaction between parkin and ubiquitinated Mfn2 – which is normally transient owing to Mfn2 turnover – was stabilized (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6J and K

claim: p97, as well as its cofactors p47 and UBXN1, are present in 4xUb pull-downs and almost totally absent in parallel 4xpUb pull-downs.
source: Using nearly fully-phosphorylated chains (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), we consistently observed the presence of p97, as well as its cofactors p47 and UBXN1, in 4xUb pull-downs, and these proteins were almost totally absent in parallel 4xpUb pull-downs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: While p97 mediates the turnover of ubiquitinated Mfn2, this likely does not involve interactions between the p97 complex and pUb.
source: Thus, while p97 mediates the turnover of ubiquitinated Mfn2, this likely does not involve interactions between the p97 complex and pUb.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p97 binds unphosphorylated Ub chains but not phosphorylated Ub chains

claim: Parkin-mediated ubiquitination on its own is insufficient to drive the disassembly of Mfn2 HMW complexes in the absence of p97 activity.
source: The herein-described role of p97 in separating mitochondria from the ER is critical; parkin-mediated ubiquitination on its own appears to be insufficient to drive the disassembly of Mfn2 HMW complexes (Figure 5E) or to dissociate the ER from the OMM (Figure 5F and G) in the absence of p97 activity.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E, F, and G

claim: In the absence of Mfn2, inhibition of p97 fails to suppress mitophagy.
source: When cells were depleted of Mfn2 (siMfn2), p97 inhibition reduced the rate of mtKeima acidification (Figure 7A and B, dark and light blue bars), but mitophagy was still permissive. Indeed, the number of cells with acidified mtKeima in siMfn2 cells treated with NMS-873 was still ~5 fold greater than their DMSO treated counterparts (Figure 7B, light blue bar), which was more of an increase that was observed for control cells with active p97 (Figure 7B, red bar). Thus, in the absence of Mfn2, inhibition of p97 fails to suppress mitophagy, demonstrating that a significant component of the role of p97 in mitophagy functions through Mfn2.
evidence: Supported by mtKeima data shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: A significant component of the role of p97 in mitophagy functions through Mfn2.
source: Thus, in the absence of Mfn2, inhibition of p97 fails to suppress mitophagy, demonstrating that a significant component of the role of p97 in mitophagy functions through Mfn2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p97 inhibition does not block mitophagy in Mfn2-depleted cells

claim: The parkin-dependent ubiquitination of VDAC1 is sensitive to p97 inhibition in control cells, but not cells depleted of Mfn2.
source: We observed that the parkin-dependent ubiquitination of VDAC1 – which has been reported to form a complex with pUb and parkin that is stable over a period of hours (Callegari et al., 2017) – was sensitive to p97 inhibition in control cells, but not cells depleted of Mfn2 (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7C-E and citation to Callegari et al., 2017

claim: The half-time of VDAC1 modification during mitophagy increases two-fold in the presence of NMS-873 specifically in control cells compared to cells transfected with siMfn2.
source: Indeed, the half-time of VDAC1 modification during mitophagy increased two-fold in the presence of NMS-873 specifically in control cells compared to cells transfected with siMfn2 (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7F

claim: Cells depleted of Mfn1 are comparable to control siRNA-transfected cells with respect to the effect of NMS-873 on VDAC1 modification.
source: Notably, cells depleted of Mfn1 were comparable to control siRNA-transfected cells in this regard (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7G and H

claim: p97 relieves Mfn2-dependent inhibition of the ubiquitination of VDAC1.
source: Thus, p97 relieves Mfn2-dependent inhibition of the ubiquitination of VDAC1 (and likely other OMM substrates).
evidence: Inferred from data showing that p97 inhibition affects VDAC1 ubiquitination in control cells but not Mfn2-depleted cells

claim: Mfn2 gates the availability of the stable parkin receptor VDAC1.
source: In this manner, Mfn2 gates the availability of the stable parkin receptor VDAC1 (Callegari et al., 2017), and mechanistically reconciles our data concerning the destruction of ER-OMM contacts during mitophagy, Mfn2-dependent mitophagy inhibition, and p97-mediated facilitation of ER-OMM uncoupling.
evidence: Inferred from data showing Mfn2-dependent effects on VDAC1 ubiquitination and citation to Callegari et al., 2017

claim: Parkin-dependent ubiquitination of Mfn2 can be reconstituted on the OMM of isolated mitochondria in a time-, depolarization- and ligase-dependent manner.
source: We were then able to reconstitute parkin-dependent ubiquitination of Mfn2 on the OMM of these isolated mitochondria by adding the E1, E2 and E3 (parkin) components of this pathway, as well as Ub and other factors, as previously described (Tang et al., 2017), in a time-, depolarization- and ligase-dependent manner (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by in organello ubiquitination data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Mfn2 ubiquitination in the in organello assay is almost completely abolished using depolarized mitochondria isolated from cells depleted of PINK1.
source: Using depolarized mitochondria isolated from cells depleted of PINK1 (Figure 8D), Mfn2 ubiquitination was almost completely abolished (Figure 8E), demonstrating an as-expected requirement for PINK1 in parkin-dependent ubiquitination.
evidence: Supported by in organello ubiquitination data shown in Figure 8D and E

claim: Cytosolic, mouse parkin is able to catalyze Mfn2 ubiquitination in a depolarization-dependent manner.
source: As parkin itself is cytosolic (Figure 8G), we initially proceeded to co-incubuate in organello ubiquitination reactions with cytosol from parkin+/+ ('WT cytosol') and parkin-/- ('KO cytosol') mouse brain in the absence of recombinant ligase, and observed that cytosolic, mouse parkin was able to catalyze Mfn2 ubiquitination in a depolarization-dependent manner, albeit not to the extent of 100 nM recombinant GST-parkin (Figure 8H; here the GST tag was not cleaved in order to visualize the different forms of parkin by immunoblot).
evidence: Supported by in organello ubiquitination data shown in Figure 8H

claim: Co-incubation of isolated mitochondria with KO cytosol and recombinant parkin results in robust ubiquitination of both Mfn2 and VDAC1 compared to reactions lacking KO cytosol.
source: Based on this result, we proceeded to co-incubate isolated mitochondria with KO cytosol and recombinant parkin. Under these conditions, we observed robust ubiquitination of both Mfn2 and VDAC1 compared to reactions lacking KO cytosol (Figure 8I).
evidence: Supported by in organello ubiquitination data shown in Figure 8I

claim: In cytosol-containing reactions, VDAC1 ubiquitination displays sensitivity to NMS-873.
source: This result indicated a potential role for p97 (which was present in the cytosol, Figure 8H and I) in this process and, remarkably, in cytosol-containing reactions, VDAC1 ubiquitination displayed sensitivity to NMS-873 (Figure 8J and K).
evidence: Supported by in organello ubiquitination data shown in Figure 8J and K

claim: NMS-873 has no effect on ubiquitination in the absence of cytosol.
source: Importantly, NMS-873 had no effect on ubiquitination in the absence of cytosol (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating that the small amount of p97 present in reactions lacking cytosol was either negligible or already engaged with other substrates.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: The addition of recombinant p97 hexamer stimulates both Mfn2 and VDAC1 ubiquitination in a parkin-dependent manner.
source: The addition of recombinant hexamer, in a parkin-dependent manner, stimulated both Mfn2 and VDAC1 ubiquitination (Figure 8M).
evidence: Supported by in organello ubiquitination data shown in Figure 8M

claim: A small amount of Mfn2 appears in the supernatant only when recombinant p97 is added to the ubiquitination reaction.
source: By fractionating samples post-reaction into mitochondria (pellet) and soluble factors (supernatant), we observed a small amount of Mfn2 appear in the supernatant only when recombinant p97 was added to the ubiquitination reaction (Figure 8N; samples were solubilized with TX-100 as a positive control).
evidence: Supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 8N

claim: Retrotranslocated Mfn2 is ubiquitinated.
source: A longer exposure revealed that retrotranslocated Mfn2 was indeed ubiquitinated (box in Figure 8N).
evidence: Supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 8N

claim: In a cell-free assay, PINK1/parkin-dependent, p97-stimulated Mfn2 and VDAC1 ubiquitination can be reconstituted.
source: Taken together, our in organello ubiquitination data show that, in a cell-free assay, we can reconstitute PINK1/parkin-dependent, p97-stimulated Mfn2 and VDAC1 ubiquitination, and Mfn2 retrotranslocation.
evidence: Supported by multiple in organello ubiquitination experiments

claim: Mfn2 retrotranslocation can be reconstituted in a cell-free assay.
source: Taken together, our in organello ubiquitination data show that, in a cell-free assay, we can reconstitute PINK1/parkin-dependent, p97-stimulated Mfn2 and VDAC1 ubiquitination, and Mfn2 retrotranslocation.
evidence: Supported by fractionation data showing p97-dependent Mfn2 retrotranslocation

claim: PINK1, parkin and p97 collaborate to uncouple OMM-ER contacts via Mfn2 ubiquitination and degradation during mitophagy.
source: These results are in line with our experiments in cells which demonstrate that PINK1, parkin and p97 collaborate to uncouple OMM-ER contacts via Mfn2 ubiquitination and degradation during mitophagy, which in turn allows ubiquitination and degradation of additional parkin substrates such as VDAC1.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments in cells and in organello assays

claim: Uncoupling of OMM-ER contacts allows ubiquitination and degradation of additional parkin substrates such as VDAC1.
source: These results are in line with our experiments in cells which demonstrate that PINK1, parkin and p97 collaborate to uncouple OMM-ER contacts via Mfn2 ubiquitination and degradation during mitophagy, which in turn allows ubiquitination and degradation of additional parkin substrates such as VDAC1.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that Mfn2 depletion or removal enhances VDAC1 ubiquitination

claim: Contacts between mitochondria and the ER are destroyed during mitophagy in both heterologous cell cultures and dopaminergic neurons.
source: Here, we have described a reciprocal relationship between mitochondria-ER tethering and mitophagy. Contacts between both organelles are destroyed during mitophagy, in both heterologous cell cultures and dopaminergic neurons, and we demonstrate a requirement for parkin, PINK1, p97 and proteasomal activity in this process.
evidence: Supported by EM data from U2OS cells and iDA neurons

claim: There is a requirement for parkin, PINK1, p97 and proteasomal activity in the destruction of mitochondria-ER contacts during mitophagy.
source: Here, we have described a reciprocal relationship between mitochondria-ER tethering and mitophagy. Contacts between both organelles are destroyed during mitophagy, in both heterologous cell cultures and dopaminergic neurons, and we demonstrate a requirement for parkin, PINK1, p97 and proteasomal activity in this process.
evidence: Supported by experiments using PINK1 depletion, parkin mutants, p97 inhibition, and proteasome inhibition

claim: Mitochondria-ER contacts are negative regulators of mitophagy.
source: Complementarily, mitochondria-ER contacts themselves are negative regulators of mitophagy, as their reduction facilitates parkin substrate ubiquitination, its translocation to mitochondria and mitochondrial turnover.
evidence: Supported by data showing enhanced mitophagy upon disruption of mitochondria-ER contacts

claim: Reduction of mitochondria-ER contacts facilitates parkin substrate ubiquitination, its translocation to mitochondria and mitochondrial turnover.
source: Complementarily, mitochondria-ER contacts themselves are negative regulators of mitophagy, as their reduction facilitates parkin substrate ubiquitination, its translocation to mitochondria and mitochondrial turnover.
evidence: Supported by data showing enhanced parkin recruitment and mitophagy in Mfn2-depleted cells

claim: Mfn2 is rapidly phosphoubiquitinated upon the induction of mitophagy.
source: We identify the known mitochondria-ER tether Mfn2 as a factor that is rapidly phosphoubiquitinated upon the induction of mitophagy, and show that Mfn2-containing HMW complexes are extracted from the OMM by p97 in a manner requiring parkin-dependent ubiquitination in the Mfn2 HR1 domain.
evidence: Supported by data showing rapid Mfn2 ubiquitination and phosphoubiquitination

claim: Mfn2-containing HMW complexes are extracted from the OMM by p97 in a manner requiring parkin-dependent ubiquitination in the Mfn2 HR1 domain.
source: We identify the known mitochondria-ER tether Mfn2 as a factor that is rapidly phosphoubiquitinated upon the induction of mitophagy, and show that Mfn2-containing HMW complexes are extracted from the OMM by p97 in a manner requiring parkin-dependent ubiquitination in the Mfn2 HR1 domain.
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data and mutagenesis experiments

claim: Both reduction of Mfn2 ubiquitination and p97 inhibition repress mitophagy.
source: Both reduction of Mfn2 ubiquitination and p97 inhibition repress mitophagy, and we reconstitute the main concepts of this PINK1/parkin/p97 enzymatic system in a cell-free assay.
evidence: Supported by data showing that Mfn2HR1 blocks mitophagy and p97 inhibition reduces mitophagy

claim: The main concepts of the PINK1/parkin/p97 enzymatic system can be reconstituted in a cell-free assay.
source: Both reduction of Mfn2 ubiquitination and p97 inhibition repress mitophagy, and we reconstitute the main concepts of this PINK1/parkin/p97 enzymatic system in a cell-free assay.
evidence: Supported by in organello ubiquitination assays

claim: The PINK1/parkin/p97 axis acts rapidly on Mfn2 HMW complexes to separate mitochondria from the ER in order to facilitate mitophagy.
source: We propose a model in which the PINK1/parkin/p97 axis acts rapidly on Mfn2 HMW complexes to separate mitochondria from the ER in order to facilitate mitophagy, potentially by making more substrates available to the parkin/PINK1 system (Figure 9).
evidence: Proposed model based on multiple experimental observations

claim: Mitochondria-ER contacts may be initial sites of PINK1/parkin activity and Ub phosphorylation.
source: Emerging from this model is the intriguing possibility that mitochondria-ER contacts are initial sites of PINK1/parkin activity and Ub phosphorylation, and would thus be critical loci of mitophagic regulation by deubiquitinating enzymes and as-yet unidentified ubiquitin phosphatases.
evidence: Speculated based on the rapid ubiquitination of Mfn2 at mitochondria-ER contacts

claim: A cryoelectron tomographical study on the ancestral yeast mitofusin Fzo1p demonstrated the existence of a ring-like structure formed by Fzo1p during the docking stage of mitochondrial fusion.
source: A recent cryoelectron tomographical study on the ancestral yeast mitofusin Fzo1p demonstrated the existence of a ring-like structure formed by Fzo1p during the docking stage of mitochondrial fusion (Brandt et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brandt et al., 2016

claim: Mfn2 bridges between mitochondria and the ER may form a similar type of ring to Fzo1p.
source: Mfn2 bridges between mitochondria and the ER may therefore form a similar type of ring, potentially restricting the availability of non-mitofusin OMM substrates such as VDAC1 (Figure 7C–H, and Figure 8I–M) to parkin and/or PINK1.
evidence: Speculated based on structural similarity to Fzo1p and data showing restricted VDAC1 ubiquitination

claim: PINK1 localizes to the mitochondria-associated membrane of the ER (MAM) upon depolarization.
source: With respect to the latter case, PINK1 has recently been shown to localize to the mitochondria-associated membrane of the ER (MAM) upon depolarization (Gelmetti et al., 2017), and a physical interaction between VDACs on the OMM and IP3 receptors on the ER places this parkin substrate at contacts between both organelles (Szabadkai et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gelmetti et al., 2017 and Szabadkai et al., 2006

claim: A physical interaction between VDACs on the OMM and IP3 receptors on the ER places VDAC1 at contacts between both organelles.
source: With respect to the latter case, PINK1 has recently been shown to localize to the mitochondria-associated membrane of the ER (MAM) upon depolarization (Gelmetti et al., 2017), and a physical interaction between VDACs on the OMM and IP3 receptors on the ER places this parkin substrate at contacts between both organelles (Szabadkai et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Szabadkai et al., 2006

claim: The existence of a ~ 500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge is supported by BN-PAGE data demonstrating that Mfn2 uniquely exists in a homotypic dimer of ~250 kDa subunits.
source: The existence of a ~ 500 kDa Mfn2-containing interorganellar bridge is supported by our BN-PAGE data (Figure 5A) demonstrating that Mfn2 uniquely exists in a homotypic dimer of ~250 kDa subunits, as it has been demonstrated that ~500 kDa mitofusin complexes form from subcomplexes on adjacent membranes (Ishihara et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Ishihara et al., 2004

claim: The observation of a steady-state ~500 kDa complex containing Mfn2 but not Mfn1 correlates with the reduced activity of the Mfn2 GTPase domain in comparison to Mfn1.
source: Our observation of a steady-state ~500 kDa complex containing Mfn2 but not Mfn1 correlates with the reduced activity of the Mfn2 GTPase domain in comparison to Mfn1 (Ishihara et al., 2004), supports a distinct role for Mfn2 in OMM-ER tethering (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and [de Brito and Scorrano, 2008]), and fits a model in which Mfns tether membranes in the GTP-bound state (Brandt et al., 2016; Ishihara et al., 2004; Qi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE data and citations to Ishihara et al., 2004; de Brito and Scorrano, 2008; Brandt et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2016

claim: The stability of Mfn2 complexes can be negatively regulated by parkin-mediated Mfn2 ubiquitination crucially coupled to p97-dependent retrotranslocation.
source: Here, we show that the stability of these complexes can be negatively regulated by parkin-mediated Mfn2 ubiquitination crucially coupled to p97-dependent retrotranslocation.
evidence: Supported by data showing p97-dependent extraction of ubiquitinated Mfn2 complexes

claim: Both ubiquitinated and unmodified forms of retrotranslocated Mfn2 are observed upon p97 addition.
source: Intriguingly, we observed both ubiquitinated and unmodified forms of retrotranslocated Mfn2 upon p97 addition (Figure 8N).
evidence: Supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 8N

claim: Ub-binding cofactors may localize the p97 hexamer to ubiquitinated Mfn2 at physiological levels of p97.
source: This may hint that, while the hexamer engages directly with Mfn2 at the high concentrations used in our assay, Ub-binding cofactors may localize the hexamer to ubiquitinated Mfn2 at physiological levels of p97.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation of both ubiquitinated and unmodified retrotranslocated Mfn2

claim: In ER-associated degradation, p97 recognizes both Ub-dependent and intrinsic signals.
source: Indeed, in ER-associated degradation, p97 recognizes both Ub-dependent and intrinsic signals (Ye et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ye et al., 2003

claim: MITOL-mediated Mfn2 ubiquitination (on different lysine residues) can positively regulate complex formation and mitochondria-ER tethering.
source: The above findings, taken together with another study demonstrating that MITOL-mediated Mfn2 ubiquitination (on different lysine residues) can positively regulate complex formation and mitochondria-ER tethering (Sugiura et al., 2013), emphasize Mfn2 ubiquitination as an important regulator of mitochondria-ER contact.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sugiura et al., 2013

claim: Mfn2 ubiquitination is an important regulator of mitochondria-ER contact.
source: The above findings, taken together with another study demonstrating that MITOL-mediated Mfn2 ubiquitination (on different lysine residues) can positively regulate complex formation and mitochondria-ER tethering (Sugiura et al., 2013), emphasize Mfn2 ubiquitination as an important regulator of mitochondria-ER contact.
evidence: Inferred from data showing parkin-mediated Mfn2 ubiquitination disrupts contacts and citation showing MITOL-mediated ubiquitination promotes contacts

claim: Robust parkin activation during mitophagy occurs through a feed-forward mechanism.
source: Robust parkin activation during mitophagy occurs through a feed-forward mechanism (Ordureau et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ordureau et al., 2014

claim: PINK1-phosphorylated Ub serves to both activate and anchor parkin to the OMM.
source: PINK1-phosphorylated Ub serves to both activate and anchor parkin to the OMM, where it can ligate more Ub moieties that are subsequently phosphorylated (Okatsu et al., 2015; Ordureau et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okatsu et al., 2015; Ordureau et al., 2014

claim: The Mfns undergo a burst of phosphoubiquitination at the onset of mitophagy, driven by localized parkin activation.
source: Here, our data hint at a hierarchy of parkin substrates. The Mfns undergo a burst of phosphoubiquitination at the onset of mitophagy, driven by localized parkin activation – potentially due to their proximity to PINK1 (Chen and Dorn, 2013).
evidence: Supported by data showing rapid Mfn ubiquitination and citation to Chen and Dorn, 2013

claim: GFP-parkin immunoprecipitation, OMM substrate turnover kinetics, and reconstitution assays show a preference for the Mfns above other parkin substrates such as HK1 and Miro1.
source: Indeed, our GFP-parkin immunoprecipitation (Figure 2C), OMM substrate turnover kinetics (Figure 2A), and reconstitution assays (Figure 8F) clearly show a preference for the Mfns above other parkin substrates such as HK1 and Miro1.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 2A, 2C, and 8F

claim: The Mfns are rapidly extracted from the OMM by p97 in a step that coincides temporally with parkin translocation to mitochondria.
source: The Mfns are then rapidly extracted from the OMM by p97 (Figure 5A and E, Figure 8N) in a step that coincides temporally with parkin translocation to mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 5A, 5E, and 8N

claim: It is unlikely that Mfn1 or Mfn2 act as a parkin receptor during mitophagy.
source: It is therefore unlikely that Mfn1 or Mfn2 act as a parkin receptor in this paradigm – as others have suggested (Chen and Dorn, 2013) – for this reason, especially when our recruitment data in Mfn2-deficient cells (Figure 3C–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4) are taken into account.
evidence: Inferred from rapid Mfn turnover and enhanced parkin recruitment in Mfn2-deficient cells

claim: Mfn2 acts as a stable parkin tether only under conditions where retrotranslocation by p97 is inhibited.
source: Indeed, we demonstrate that Mfn2 acts as a stable parkin tether only under conditions where retrotranslocation by p97 is inhibited (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6J and K

claim: VDAC1 is involved in a stable complex that tethers parkin to the OMM.
source: Our data support a role for the involvement of VDAC1 in a stable complex that tethers parkin to the OMM (Callegari et al., 2017); as β-barrel channels fully integrated into the membrane, VDACs may not be amenable to p97-dependent retrotranslocation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Callegari et al., 2017 and inference about VDAC structure

claim: Mfn2 may act as a parkin receptor in cardiomyocytes.
source: Mfn2 may act as a parkin receptor in cardiomyocytes (Chen and Dorn, 2013), where parkin-dependent clearance of mitochondria by autophagy plays a role in metabolic development (Gong et al., 2015) rather than quality control, and thus may occur by a distinct mechanism; the phosphomutant Mfn2T111A/S442A or Mfn2 deletion blocks parkin-mediated mitophagy in the heart but not in cell lines (Figure 4J and K, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and [Narendra et al., 2008]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Dorn, 2013; Gong et al., 2015; Narendra et al., 2008 and data shown in Figures 4J, K, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Phosphorylation of Mfn2 on T111 and S442 by a cardiac-specific S/T kinase may facilitate mitophagy in the heart by uncoupling mitochondria from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
source: Conceivably, phosphorylation of Mfn2 on T111 and S442 by a cardiac-specific S/T kinase (or cardiac PINK1, as has been proposed [Chen and Dorn, 2013]) may facilitate mitophagy in the heart by uncoupling mitochondria from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: Speculated based on tissue-specific differences in Mfn2 phosphomutant effects

claim: Mitophagy functions as a quality control mechanism.
source: Our study describes an antagonistic, reciprocal relationship between mitophagy and interorganellar tethering between mitochondria and the ER. This highlights a fundamental difference between mitophagy and the more canonical starvation-induced autophagy pathway, the latter of which requires mitochondria-ER contact sites for autophagosome formation (Hamasaki et al., 2013). While mitophagy functions as a quality control mechanism (Ryan et al., 2015), starvation-induced autophagy is a metabolic response, and thus its initiation at contact sites between mitochondria and the ER may serve to decode the metabolic needs of the cell.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2015

claim: Starvation-induced autophagy is a metabolic response.
source: While mitophagy functions as a quality control mechanism (Ryan et al., 2015), starvation-induced autophagy is a metabolic response, and thus its initiation at contact sites between mitochondria and the ER may serve to decode the metabolic needs of the cell.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about autophagy

claim: Initiation of starvation-induced autophagy at contact sites between mitochondria and the ER may serve to decode the metabolic needs of the cell.
source: While mitophagy functions as a quality control mechanism (Ryan et al., 2015), starvation-induced autophagy is a metabolic response, and thus its initiation at contact sites between mitochondria and the ER may serve to decode the metabolic needs of the cell.
evidence: Speculated based on the metabolic nature of starvation-induced autophagy

claim: Both mitochondria and the ER have been reported to function as autophagosomal membrane sources during starvation.
source: Mechanistically, both mitochondria (Hailey et al., 2010) and the ER (Hayashi-Nishino et al., 2009) have been reported to function as autophagosomal membrane sources during starvation, and mitochondrial damage may preclude the former from participating in this process during mitophagy.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hailey et al., 2010 and Hayashi-Nishino et al., 2009

claim: Mitochondrial damage may preclude mitochondria from participating as an autophagosomal membrane source during mitophagy.
source: Mechanistically, both mitochondria (Hailey et al., 2010) and the ER (Hayashi-Nishino et al., 2009) have been reported to function as autophagosomal membrane sources during starvation, and mitochondrial damage may preclude the former from participating in this process during mitophagy.
evidence: Speculated based on the damaged state of mitochondria during mitophagy

claim: The SNARE Stx17 governs autophagosome-lysosome fusion during starvation.
source: Accordingly, the SNARE Stx17, which governs autophagosome-lysosome fusion during starvation (Itakura et al., 2012b), is dispensable for mitophagy (McLelland et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Itakura et al., 2012b; McLelland et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016

claim: Stx17 is dispensable for mitophagy.
source: Accordingly, the SNARE Stx17, which governs autophagosome-lysosome fusion during starvation (Itakura et al., 2012b), is dispensable for mitophagy (McLelland et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to McLelland et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016

claim: Stx17 suppresses mitophagy through its role in supporting mitochondria-ER contact.
source: Indeed, Stx17 appears to suppress mitophagy (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G–I) through its role in supporting mitochondria-ER contact (Arasaki et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G-I and citation to Arasaki et al., 2015

claim: Mitophagy shares morphological and several mechanistic similarities with canonical macroautophagy, including the recruitment of ULK1 complexes and ATG9A vesicles to depolarized mitochondria.
source: While mitophagy does indeed share morphological and several mechanistic similarities with canonical macroautophagy – including the recruitment of ULK1 complexes and ATG9A vesicles to depolarized mitochondria (Itakura et al., 2012a; Lazarou et al., 2015) – molecular dissection of mitophagosome formation and fusion requires further study.
evidence: Supported by citations to Itakura et al., 2012a; Lazarou et al., 2015

claim: Phenotypes of PINK1 and PRKN mutants in flies are duplicated by overexpression of the sole Drosophila mitofusin MARF.
source: In flies, phenotypes of PINK1 and PRKN mutants are duplicated by overexpression of the sole Drosophila mitofusin MARF, and are suppressed by p97 overexpression (Yun et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yun et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017

claim: Phenotypes of PINK1 and PRKN mutants in flies are suppressed by p97 overexpression.
source: In flies, phenotypes of PINK1 and PRKN mutants are duplicated by overexpression of the sole Drosophila mitofusin MARF, and are suppressed by p97 overexpression (Yun et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yun et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017

claim: PINK1/parkin/p97 counteract MARF in vivo through its ubiquitination and turnover.
source: Thus, PINK1/parkin/p97 counteract MARF in vivo through its ubiquitination and turnover (Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017; Ziviani et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017; Ziviani et al., 2010

claim: A proposed mechanism of cell death due to deletion of PINK1 is the sensitization of mitochondria to Ca2+ overload.
source: Indeed, a proposed mechanism of cell death due to deletion of PINK1 is the sensitization of mitochondria to Ca2+ overload (Akundi et al., 2011; Gandhi et al., 2009; Kostic et al., 2015), the root cause of which may be dysregulation of mitochondria-ER contact.
evidence: Supported by citations to Akundi et al., 2011; Gandhi et al., 2009; Kostic et al., 2015

claim: Deletion of the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter protects dopaminergic neurons from cell death in PINK1-deficient zebrafish.
source: Accordingly, deletion of the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter protects dopaminergic neurons from cell death in PINK1-deficient zebrafish (Soman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Soman et al., 2017

claim: An increased degree of mitochondria-ER contact and metabolite transfer has been observed in both fibroblasts from PRKN and PINK1 patients, as well as brains from PINK1 and PRKN mutant flies.
source: While we did not observe any steady-state differences in the extent of mitochondria-ER coupling in either parkin overexpression (Figure 1A–E) or loss-of-function (Figure 1N and O) systems, others have observed an increased degree of contact and metabolite transfer in both fibroblasts from PRKN and PINK1 patients, as well as brains from PINK1 and PRKN mutant flies (Celardo et al., 2016; Gautier et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Celardo et al., 2016; Gautier et al., 2016

claim: Transient depletion of PINK1 destabilizes mitochondria-ER tethering.
source: Conversely, we (Figure 1H–J) and others (Gelmetti et al., 2017) measured a destabilization of mitochondria-ER tethering when PINK1 was transiently depleted.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H-J and citation to Gelmetti et al., 2017
